When the imam says Allah listens to him who praises Him, or ends the Fatiha, those behind respond with praise and Amin; whoever matches the angels is forgiven past sins.
Hurt by a fall from his horse or ill, the Prophet led prayer sitting and seated those behind: the imam is to be followed, never preceded, sitting when he sits.
In his last illness the Prophet had Abu Bakr lead the prayer despite Aisha's objections, once prayed seated beside him, and on Monday looked at the rows and died.
In the Prophet's absence Abu Bakr and Abd al-Rahman b. Auf began leading the prayer before he arrived; to alert the imam men glorify Allah, while clapping is for women.
The Prophet told people to perform their bowing and prostration well, saying he saw them behind his back as he saw in front.
The Prophet forbade preceding the imam in bowing, prostration or standing, said he had seen Paradise and Hell, and warned Allah may turn a head raised first into an ass's.
Worshippers must not lift their eyes to the sky in prayer or wave their hands at the salutation like headstrong horses' tails, but be calm and form rows like angels.
The Prophet straightened the rows like an arrow, warning that crooked rows bring dissension among hearts, and wanted the sedate and prudent nearest him.
If people knew the first row's merit they would draw lots for it; men's best rows are first, women's last, and women were once told to lift heads after men.
The Prophet said not to prevent women from going to the mosque, even at night, when they ask; Ibn Umar harshly rebuked his son for saying he would prevent them.
A woman coming to the mosque or the Isha prayer must not wear perfume; Aisha said that had the Prophet seen what women introduced, he would have prevented them.
Ibn Abbas says the verse on praying neither too loudly nor too low came while the Prophet hid in Mecca and polytheists reviled the Quran; Aisha says it concerns supplication.
The Prophet moved his tongue to memorise revelation as Gabriel brought it, until Allah told him not to hasten, for He would collect it; then he listened and afterwards recited.
Told by a verse not to move his tongue in haste, the Prophet listened attentively while Gabriel recited and, when Gabriel left, recited as he had.
Jinn heard the Prophet reciting at the morning prayer and believed; one night he went with their inviter, recited the Quran to them, and named bones as their food.
In noon and afternoon prayers the Prophet recited al-Fatiha and a surah in the first two rak'ahs, longer than the last two, as Sa'd told Umar he too did.
In the morning prayer the Prophet recited Surah Qaf, al-Mu'minun and the like, sixty to a hundred verses, prolonging it more than the noon and afternoon prayers.
The Prophet recited Surat al-Tur and the surah Umm al-Fadl last heard from him in the evening prayer, and 'By the Fig' in the night prayer on a journey.
When Mu'adh, after praying with the Prophet, led his people in a long night prayer with al-Baqara, the Prophet rebuked him for trying them and named shorter surahs to recite.
An imam must be brief for the weak, sick, aged and busy, but alone one may lengthen; the Prophet's prayer was brief yet perfect, shortened when a child cried.
The Prophet's standing, bowing, rising, prostrating and sitting were nearly balanced, and he and Anas paused after bowing and between prostrations so long that people thought they had forgotten.
Behind the Prophet no one bent down for prostration until he had placed his forehead on the ground; only then did they follow him.
On rising from bowing the Prophet praised his Lord with praise filling the heavens and earth, saying none can withhold what He gives, and asked to be purified with snow.
The Prophet said only good visions remain of prophethood's glad tidings and forbade reciting the Quran in bowing and prostration, which are for glorifying the Lord and supplication.
A servant is nearest his Lord in prostration, so supplicate there; bowing and prostrating, the Prophet glorified Allah, asked forgiveness and sought refuge in His pleasure from His anger.
Frequent prostration raises a degree and removes a sin with each one, and the Prophet told Rabi'a, who asked for his company in Paradise, to help him by prostrating often.
The Prophet was commanded to prostrate on seven bones, forehead, hands, knees and feet, and not to fold back hair or clothing; Ibn Abbas undid a man's plaited hair.
In prostration the forearms are not spread like a dog's: palms down, elbows raised, the Prophet's arms so wide his armpits showed; Aisha described his prayer from takbir to taslim.
A sutra the height of a saddle's back suffices; the Prophet prayed facing a planted spear, staff or his camel, while people and animals passed beyond it.
Nearly of age, Ibn Abbas rode a donkey in front of the row as the Prophet led prayer at Mina, then joined it, and no one objected.
A worshipper must turn back, forcibly if needed, anyone passing before him; a passer knowing his burden would rather stand forty; the Prophet prayed near a wall or pillar.
Without a saddle-high sutra a passing woman, ass or black dog cuts the prayer; Aisha objected that the Prophet prayed at night while she lay between him and the qibla.
Asked about praying in one garment, the Prophet asked if everyone had two, and he himself prayed in a single garment, its ends crossed over his shoulders.
The first mosque on earth was al-Masjid al-Haram, then al-Aqsa forty years later, and wherever the time of prayer comes, the earth is a mosque.
The Prophet and his community were given what others were not: mission to all mankind, lawful spoils, the earth as mosque and purifier, terror in enemies' hearts, intercession, concise speech.
Arriving in Medina, the Prophet prayed in sheepfolds until the Banu al-Najjar gave their land for Allah's reward and he had it cleared to build the mosque.
After sixteen or seventeen months of praying towards Bait-ul-Maqdis, the qibla was changed to the Ka'ba, and people at prayer, told of it, turned round in mid-prayer.
The Prophet called builders of places of worship on pious men's graves the worst of creatures, cursed Jews and Christians who took their prophets' graves as mosques, and forbade it.
When people objected to Uthman rebuilding the Prophet's mosque, he cited the Prophet: whoever builds a mosque for Allah, Allah builds for him a house like it in Paradise.
Ibn Mas'ud bowed with palms between his thighs, but Sa'd said this was later replaced by palms on the knees; Ibn Abbas called a sitting hard on the foot sunnah.
